Last time we asked which of two tunings sounds better, 432 Hz or 440 Hz, and your answers varied a lot. “Sounding better” is highly subjective, so there is no right answer. In today’s sequel I take a purely objective angle and look at a little of the acoustics behind musical instruments.

432 Hz or 440 Hz: which sounds better?

On a piano, take the seven white keys and five black keys in the figure below: twelve keys in all, making up one octave. Adjacent keys are a semitone apart, and keys two apart are a whole tone apart. Taking C major as an example, you probably know the names of the white keys: the seven notes Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Si, which some countries call C, D, E, F, G, A, B. The black keys have no names of their own. They are named after a neighboring note plus a sharp (#) or flat (b). The first black key from the left, for example, can be called Do-sharp, C# (which has nothing whatsoever to do with the programming language C#), or Re-flat, Db.

Now extend this to the whole 88-key piano. Divide the keyboard into regions, one color each, and you can see that every region repeats the pattern of keys above. Moving from left to right, each note in a region is an octave above the corresponding note in the region to its left, and its frequency is twice as high.

Sharp-eyed readers will spot the star of the previous article: the standard pitch A4. As you can see at a glance, A4 is the A (La) in the fourth octave. So the frequency of A4 is twice that of A3 and half that of A5.

None of this is unique to the piano; it applies to other instruments too. Take the guitar. Its six strings are tuned to six notes spread across three octaves, and each fret (the boxes in the figure) is a semitone apart, just like adjacent piano keys. So if you start on the first fret of the sixth string (F2) and want the F3 an octave higher, you move up the same string to the 13th fret.

The same rule for every instrument

It feels natural to assume that as you play a piano from left to right, the frequency rises linearly. It doesn’t. Frequency grows exponentially as the notes go up; in other words, it rises on a logarithmic scale. What is a logarithmic scale? One where the ratio between neighboring marks is constant, whereas on a linear scale the difference is constant. Why bother with a logarithmic scale? Because the ear perceives frequency logarithmically. I won’t go into how the ear perceives sound here.

When we listen to C4–G4 and C6–G6, for example, what we hear is not the difference between their frequencies but the ratio.

Try it yourself with the video below. We can clearly hear the difference between 300 Hz and 600 Hz, because one is twice the other: an octave apart. The difference between 2300 Hz and 2600 Hz is much less obvious. They are also 300 Hz apart, but the ratio is only 1.13, so they are harder to tell apart.

Back to the standard pitch A4. Once the international standard A4 = 440 Hz is fixed, how do we work out the other notes? The A’s in other octaves are easy, but what about the rest?

As we just saw, the ear perceives frequency on a logarithmic scale, and on a logarithmic scale neighboring values are related by a ratio. So the twelve notes in an octave are separated by a frequency ratio of 212: each note’s frequency is 212 times that of the note before it. Multiply the twelve steps of an octave together, (212)12=2, and you get the same conclusion as before: notes an octave apart differ in frequency by a factor of two. Dividing the octave into equal steps like this is called twelve-tone equal temperament.
